svg.text: THE JOINTS AGAINST THE LIMB, TO SCALE
The fork is the whole limb with a slot through it, and the tongue is what the slot took out.
Four springs, in two pairs: an ear and a leaf on each side, sharing the movement between them.
Ø24 mm limb, Ø12.16 mm cavity
leaves 5.92 mm of wall
flat top and bottom, 20.9 mm
slot 11.8 mm through a 24 mm limb
ear 6.1 either side, tongue 10 between
split by a 1.6 slit into two leaves, 4.2 at the root
BALL AND SOCKET, IN SECTION
socket — the outboard part
cavity Ø12.16 mm
= ball + 2 × fit
grip 2.22 mm — sets the mouth
mouth Ø11.32 mm — 94% of the ball
ball Ø12 mm
stalk Ø6 mm
ball stud — the inboard part
The ball stud goes on the part nearer the torso, the socket on the part further out. Always.
Clearance drawn oversize to be visible; every number here is the real one.
HINGE — TWO RINGS OF WEDGES
ALONG THE LIMB
ONE EAR, INSIDE
fork — two ears
wedge — 45° sides, 0.75 mm proud
bore Ø4.1 mm through each ear
axle Ø4 mm, 3 mm proud
slit 1.6 mm at the root, 7 at the tip
24 wedges, 15° apart, r 6 to 10.45 mm
the face: one plane, 20.9 mm across,
standing 0.9 mm off the tongue’s
dashed: where the tongue’s 24 wedges sit, half a step round
Elbows and knees. Pinch the two leaves together, slide the tongue in, and let go — the axle springs into the bores and the two rings drop into step.
The two faces never touch. They stand 0.9 mm apart, which is one wedge plus 0.15 mm of air over its tip, and every protrusion in the joint
is a wedge: there are no holes to clean out. Both members are cut off 15 mm from the pin here:
the tongue roots 20 mm out and the ear 21, and those two lengths are the spring.
75.22 N to pinch together; 1332.32 N·mm to turn, which is 51.24 times what holding the arm up takes.
SHEET 2 — THE UNIQUE PARTS
One of each goes in the Part Studio; the assembly makes the copies.
A + marks a joint part: modeled on its own, then added to the part it sits on. A socket is added too, even though it cuts material away.
Every ball stud stands off its face on a stalk, as drawn here. On sheet 1 the joint centers sit on their station lines instead — that is the kinematic view.
Where the two sheets disagree, this one is the one to build from.

The hip stud stands off the torso’s bottom face like every other, and the leg drops the 10 mm with it. A recess into the torso was considered and dropped: it buys no swing, because the 39.01° limit is set inside the socket, by the stalk meeting the mouth.

The shoulder is the exception. Its stud runs 26 mm from the side face, of which only the last 10 is Ø6; the rest is a Ø16 boss on the same axis, cut off flush where it crosses the top face. Coaxial is what makes the boss free: it sits behind the ball, and the socket only reaches forward of it.

The hinge divides the same Ø24 three ways: ear 6.1, tongue 10, ear 6.1, and a slit splits the tongue again into two leaves, 4.2 thick at the root and 1.5 at the tip. So each side of the joint is two springs in series, an ear and a leaf, and they share the

0.6 mm a wedge needs. Turning it takes 1332.32 N·mm, which is 51.24 times what holding the arm up takes, and only 4 of the 24 wedges carry it. Pinching it together takes 75.22 N, which is the harder case at 38.34 MPa against PETG’s 50.
